title: Aditi's milk vow
hookLine: a mother can't win back her sons' loss, so she keeps a vow
carry: a vrata puts in God's hands what you can't fix
tomorrow: the promised son is tiny. so what does he ask the king for?

lines: YOU CAN'T FIX IT FOR THEM.
cards: There's a particular helplessness in watching someone you love lose something you can't get back for them: a job, a place on a team, a home. In the Bhagavata Purana, that's Aditi.
Her sons are the gods, and they've just lost heaven. Prahlada's grandson, Bali, a generous king of the asuras, has taken it, and the gods are in hiding. Aditi can't fight him.
She can't fix it. So she sits at home, and grieves.

teach.h: HE LISTENS. HE DOESN'T FIX IT.
teach.b: Then her husband, the sage Kashyapa, comes home and finds the house gone quiet. He listens. He doesn't promise to fix it.
Instead he gives her a vrata, a vow, to Vishnu: for the days of the vow she lives on milk and worships him each day.
The text calls it payovrata, the milk vow. So Aditi keeps it, day after day. And at the end, Vishnu appears to her and promises: he'll be born as her son.
When that son arrives, he's small, a young student who, in the telling, is given an umbrella and a water pot. His name is Vamana, the small one. Here's the teaching.
Many teachers put it this way: a vrata isn't a bribe, and it isn't a fix.

teach.h: A VRATA: PUT IT IN GOD'S HANDS.
teach.b: It's what a Hindu does when a thing is too big to carry: you take a vow, keep it steadily, and put what you can't fix in God's hands.
Aditi's story is one of the old pictures of it, and the practice is still everywhere.
Many Hindu mothers and grandmothers keep vratas for their children, a fast on a set day, a lamp, a prayer, often without telling anyone. And when help comes, it rarely comes the way anyone planned.
Here, it comes small enough to hold.

how: Some Hindus keep a vrata, a vow of fasting or simple worship over set days, for a family member in trouble; keeping the vow steadily is itself the offering.

o: the vow of milk that Aditi kept
Vishnu as a small boy, a young dwarf student
a giant who guards the gate of heaven

games.q: who's who in the loss — tap the pairs.
p: listens, then gives her a vow

s: Bali is a cruel tyrant, like Hiranyakashipu
the Purana calls him generous. the next days show how he keeps his word.
Aditi goes to war to win heaven back for her sons
she can't fight. she keeps a small, steady vow.
Bali, who holds heaven, is Prahlada's grandson
the story moves two generations on from Narasimha.

games.q: your aunt fasts one day a week while her son is in the hospital. a friend asks, 'does skipping lunch fix anything?' by Aditi's story?
o: it's a vrata: not a fix, a steady vow that puts it in God's hands.
yes: fast hard enough and God has to give you what you want.
no; it's an old diet custom with no meaning behind it.
games.why: Aditi couldn't win heaven back. she kept the milk vow to Vishnu, steadily, and left the rest to him.

practice: Think of one person carrying a loss you can't fix. Choose a tiny vow for them, small enough to keep: a lamp or candle each evening this week, a short prayer at bedtime, or, if you don't pray, one kind message each evening.
Make the promise once, silently. Then give a few slow breaths to holding them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Vamana: Vishnu as the small one, a young dwarf student, born to Aditi after her steady vow.
